presentingComplaint: Progressive confusion, drowsiness and disturbed sleep-wake pattern over 3 days in a man with known alcohol-related cirrhosis.
history: 58-year-old man with biopsy-proven alcohol-related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, prior grade 1-2 encephalopathy) and type 2 diabetes on metformin. Brought by family with 3 days of increasing confusion, daytime somnolence with nocturnal restlessness, irritability and one episode of getting lost in his own home. He had stopped his lactulose 5 days ago because of loose stools and has been constipated since, opening his bowels only once in 4 days. No haematemesis or melaena reported. No fever, cough, dysuria or diarrhoea. Family confirm he has not had alcohol for 2 months. Recent addition of an over-the-counter diuretic and reduced oral intake. No new sedatives beyond his usual. Background: two prior variceal bandings, ascites managed with spironolactone, no prior overt GI bleed this admission. The overlapping features (a cirrhotic patient who is also diabetic, mildly hyponatraemic and drowsy) raise metabolic and toxic causes, but the picture is dominated by an asterixis-positive fluctuating encephalopathy in decompensated cirrhosis with a clear precipitant (constipation + lactulose cessation + diuretic-induced volume/electrolyte shift).
examination: Drowsy but rousable to voice, disoriented to time and place, GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6). Coarse flapping tremor (asterixis) of outstretched hands. Fetor hepaticus. Icteric sclerae, spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia. Abdomen distended with moderate ascites and shifting dullness, non-tender, no guarding; no rebound. No abdominal wall erythema. Mild pedal oedema. No neck stiffness, no focal neurological deficit, plantars flexor, pupils equal and reactive. Capillary blood glucose 7.8 mmol/L. No rash, no track marks. Chest clear, no signs of aspiration.
imaging: Ultrasound abdomen: coarse nodular shrunken liver, splenomegaly, moderate ascites, patent portal vein, no focal liver lesion, no biliary dilatation. CT head (to exclude structural cause of altered sensorium): age-appropriate atrophy, no haemorrhage, mass or infarct.
microbiology: Diagnostic ascitic tap: PMN count 90 cells/mm3 (<250, excludes SBP), culture no growth. Blood cultures negative. Urinalysis unremarkable. No microbiological evidence of infection driving the presentation.
differentialDiagnoses: Hepatic encephalopathy precipitated by constipation, lactulose cessation and diuretic use (working diagnosis)
Wernicke encephalopathy in a chronic alcohol user
Occult spontaneous bacterial peritonitis precipitating encephalopathy (excluded by ascitic tap)
finalDiagnosis: Overt hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade 2) in decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis, precipitated by constipation, lactulose non-adherence and diuretic-related electrolyte disturbance.
citations: AASLD/EASL Practice Guideline: Hepatic Encephalopathy in Chronic Liver Disease 2014
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22e - Cirrhosis and its Complications
EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Decompensated Cirrhosis 2018
stewardship: Non-infective decompensation. No empiric antibiotics indicated once SBP and other sepsis are excluded (afebrile, normal WBC/CRP, ascitic PMN <250, negative cultures). Management is precipitant-directed: lactulose titrated to 2-3 soft stools/day (initial dose then maintenance), add rifaximin 550 mg BD as gut-directed therapy for recurrent HE, correct hyponatraemia cautiously, withhold the offending diuretic, ensure nutrition (avoid protein restriction) and thiamine cover given alcohol history. Antibiotics would only be added if a source of infection emerged.
contraindications: Avoid protein restriction - worsens malnutrition without benefit
Avoid benzodiazepines/sedatives - precipitate and deepen encephalopathy
Correct hyponatraemia slowly (<8-10 mmol/L/24h) to avoid osmotic demyelination
Caution with further diuresis given volume/electrolyte contribution
Avoid nephrotoxins/NSAIDs given cirrhosis and risk of hepatorenal syndrome
edgeCases: If ascitic PMN had been >=250/mm3, SBP would be the precipitant requiring cefotaxime
Overt GI bleed as precipitant would mandate endoscopy and would shift priority to variceal management
Persistent confusion despite normal ammonia and cleared precipitants should prompt re-imaging and EEG for non-convulsive status or structural cause
Refractory/recurrent HE despite lactulose+rifaximin raises consideration of large portosystemic shunt and transplant assessment
expectedMaiK: Recognise overt hepatic encephalopathy as a clinical diagnosis in decompensated cirrhosis (asterixis, fetor, fluctuating sensorium with a clear precipitant), actively identify and reverse precipitants, and treat with lactulose +/- rifaximin rather than reflexively starting antibiotics.
expectedNextQuestions: Adherence to lactulose and stool frequency in recent days?
Any haematemesis, melaena or recent GI bleeding?
New sedatives, opioids or diuretics; alcohol relapse?
Any fever or symptoms suggesting infection/SBP?
expectedInvestigations: Diagnostic ascitic tap with cell count and culture
Serum electrolytes, renal function and glucose
LFTs, INR and full blood count
CT head to exclude structural cause of altered sensorium
